headline: SW Ledge Slack at 5:52: Bass Buried Deep, Blues on Top, Bonito Still a Question Mark
subhead: The ledge is fishing on a ten-minute window right now — everything else is happening after dark or up top on bait.
body_markdown:
5:52 AM. That's when the tide goes slack at SW Ledge this week, and if you want a real shot at a daytime striper off that structure, that ten-minute window around the turn is your play. I ran out there Tuesday morning, watched the sonar light up on the down-current face at 52 feet right as the current died, worked a bucktail through it for maybe eight minutes — one fish, a schoolie that came unbuttoned at the boat — and then the tide swung and every mark on the screen dropped back into the rocks like someone pulled a curtain. That's the ledge right now. It's not dead, it's disciplined.

Here's the why. Surface water on both sides of the Block — Montauk's reading 69.1, and I'd put SW Ledge and the west side of the island in that same neighborhood, maybe a degree warmer in the afternoon sun. That's warm enough that the bass have gone almost entirely nocturnal. Daytime, they're holding tight to structure and current seams — the down-tide face of the ledge, the humps off Southwest, the deeper cuts around Sandy Point — and they're not interested in chasing much until the sun's off the water. After dark is a different story. Guys working bunker chunks on fishfinder rigs off the ledge in 45 to 60 feet, and guys swimming eels along the rock piles at Sandy Point and off North Light, are still connecting with real fish — some pushing 30 pounds, a few better. If you want a daytime bite right now, the slack window is genuinely your best shot; if you want numbers, you're fishing at night.

Fluke have done exactly what fluke do when the shallow water gets warm and sleepy — they've pushed off the flats and into the deeper channel bends where there's still moving, cooler water. The Harbor of Refuge drop and the deeper stretch along the West Wall have been the most consistent producers, along with the edge off Whale Rock where the bottom breaks toward 30-35 feet. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, dragged slow on the last two hours of the ebb — that's been the combination putting keepers in the box, mixed in with a lot of throwbacks. It's not a wide-open bite. You're covering ground to find the pockets, but there are fish there if you're willing to move.

apBluefish are the one thing that's been unambiguous. Bunker schools have been running thick along the beachfront from the Galilee breakwater down toward Sandy Point, and where that bait gets pinned against structure on a moving tide, the blues have been blitzing hard — birds working, fish busting bait right on the surface. I had a charter into that Wednesday off Sandy Point on the last of the incoming, popping topwater plugs and Deadly Dicks into the melee, and we lost count of fish in under an hour. If you see the birds diving and the water nervous, don't overthink it — get a metal in there fast before the school moves.

Black sea bass have quietly been the most dependable bite in the whole zone. The reef structure around SW Ledge and the rockier bottom off Block's southwest corner, working 80 to 100 feet, has been holding solid numbers of keeper sea bass on squid strips and clam bellies fished on a standard two-hook bottom rig. It's not glamorous, but it's about as close to a sure thing as this zone offers right now, and it's a good fallback plan on a day when the top-water bite is slow.

Now, the one everybody's asking me about at the dock — bonito. Not yet. Water temps on both sides of the Block have crossed the threshold where they typically show, and we flagged that arrival window a few days back expecting it to come due about now. It hasn't happened yet in this zone, at least not that I've confirmed with my own eyes or a rod bent over it. What I can tell you is the moon's waxing toward full in early August, which means the current through the rips — SW Ledge, the rip off North Light, the water off Clay Head — is about to build noticeably. That's exactly the mechanism that concentrates bait and triggers that first bonito showing. If I had to bet, I'd watch the surface around North Light and off Southeast Light on a building tide over the next week, small Deadly Dicks and epoxy jigs rigged and ready in the console. But I'm not going to tell you they're here when they're not.

Looking ahead: I'd fish the slack windows at SW Ledge for daytime bass, shift to eels and chunks after dark for the better fish, keep working the deeper fluke edges on the ebb, and stay ready for that first bonito flash the moment the current sharpens up toward the full moon. It's a working week, not a gimme — but there's enough happening across the board to make the run out of Galilee worth it if you pick your tide and stick to the plan.
